blocks.text: 3. What Mind Is to Be Contemplated

inline.s: A Treatise on Arousing the Bodhi Mind says:
"When the deluded mind arises, know it and do not follow it; when it subsides, the source of the mind is empty and still, all virtues are complete, and its wondrous functions are inexhaustible."

Such is the wonder of the mind-nature. That we are ordinarily out of accord with it is because we are obscured by deluded thought, which is the ignorant mind. On what does ignorance rely? It arises in dependence upon suchness. To contemplate the ignorant mind is to contemplate the mind of suchness; to contemplate the mind-nature is to contemplate the ignorant mind. Why? Because suchness is the substance of thought, and thought is the function of suchness. To contemplate and thereby attain concentration is the samadhi of suchness, the king of all samadhis, and this is why it is called the supreme concentration.

What mind is to be contemplated? It is said: contemplate the ignorant mind. Why not contemplate the true mind? Because since the beginningless past the true mind has been perfumed and obscured by ignorance and cannot manifest. Where does this ignorance dwell? It dwells upon the true mind, like glue sticking to lacquer, never able to gain release; therefore it is called the ignorance that abides in the ground. This ignorance is the root of birth-and-death; while a single part of it remains unexhausted, birth-and-death forever continues, and so it is called fundamental ignorance. One who studies the Dharma and seeks the truth must begin with this ignorance that abides in the ground. Why? If when felling a tree one does not cut its root, or when treating an illness one does not strike the right point, then it avails nothing at all. Therefore those of the Two Vehicles and the bodhisattvas of the provisional teaching may sever the four abiding ignorances, yet they do not know the ignorance that abides in the ground; they can escape birth-and-death by divisions but in the end still undergo birth-and-death by transformation. One who follows the One Vehicle begins with contemplating the mind in order to break the ignorance that abides in the ground, so that birth-and-death is cut off forever; this is what is meant by drawing blood from the throat, the marvelous formula for becoming a Buddha, the most genuine and the most real. Elder Li says:
"Fundamental ignorance is none other than the fundamental, unmoving wisdom."
Yongjia says:
"The real nature of ignorance is itself the Buddha-nature."
The Tiantai school says:
"The substance of ignorance is itself illumination, itself reality, itself the Dharma-nature."

The scriptures quote this in endless profusion, and all point to this very point. At first, contemplate the mind that arises and ceases, without grasping or clinging, without following it or cutting it off; or give yourself over wholly to stilling thought and forgetting deliberation; and the two methods are one. (The Essentials of the Mind-Dharma Transmission says:
"Still thought and forget deliberation, and the Buddha appears of itself before you."

To contemplate and reflect constantly is to perfume ignorance with prajna. The very moment ignorance is broken, the dharmakaya suddenly manifests. In one leap one enters directly the ground of the Tathagata; without passing through asankhya kalpas one attains the dharmakaya; and so it is called the perfect and sudden gate of the Dharma.

Choose a clean and quiet place and sit in the full lotus posture. (First press the left foot upon the right thigh, then press the right foot upon the left thigh, so that the soles of both feet face upward upon the two thighs. Place the hands likewise, right over left, resting upon the upturned crossed legs. This is the full lotus, called the auspicious sitting. Or one may use only the half lotus, resting the right foot upon the left thigh, which is also acceptable. There is moreover the demon-subduing sitting: first press the right foot upon the left thigh, then the left foot upon the right thigh, with the hands left over right; the Chan school has for the most part transmitted this posture, so let each person choose as he wishes. The aged may sit upright and simple instead.) Keep the body upright and straight, neither moving nor swaying. Form the concentration mudra with the hands. (Turn both palms upward, the right hand placed over the left, the tips of the two thumbs touching, and rest them below the navel upon the crossed legs. This is called the dharma-realm concentration mudra, and it can dispel all wild and deluded thoughts.) Close the eyes to cut off the light, close the mouth and join the teeth, keep the tongue against the upper palate, and let the nose face the navel. Keep the spine straight as a rod and the two shoulders level, without leaning or tilting, and so sit.

For those busy with affairs, one must sit once a day, at least half an hour each time. If one can sit two or three times, each for an hour or two, that is even better. The more often and the longer, the better. When sitting, loosen the clothes and slacken the belt, calm and at ease, and do not sit in a draft, nor after a full meal. When the sitting is completed, gently move the body, slowly open the eyes and mouth, rub the two hands together until warm, and massage the face, eyes, waist, abdomen, legs, and feet; rest a while, and then rise.
Question: Because of the limitations of my body I am unable to sit in the lotus posture. What shall I do?

Answer: You may use the loose cross-legged position, with the two legs crossed, or sit upright upon a chair or stool; whatever the posture, keep the back straight, though without thrusting the chest out too far, and adopt the one that is stable and can be sustained for long.
Question: When contemplating the mind, must I always form the mudra?
Answer: One may contemplate the mind without forming the mudra.
Question: When the contemplation of mind is finished, to where should I dedicate the merit?

Answer: To contemplate the mind is itself the dedication of merit to the true reality of suchness, for the other Buddhas and one's own Buddha are one body; what further doubt could there be? Since you have newly entered the Dharma gate, dedicating the merit to the other Buddhas is also acceptable.

blocks.text: 5. Contemplating the Mind Off the Cushion

inline.s: In contemplating the mind, the crucial point is that it be continuous and unbroken, never forgotten. The ancients said:
"If a single thought is not present
(the thought of contemplation is not present)
, one is the same as a dead man."

The essential instruction of contemplating the mind is this: one can contemplate the mind anywhere at any time, and one is always contemplating the mind, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, never apart from the present thought, ever the master of oneself. When the practice reaches this point, its wonder is so deep and vast as to be without limit, like water drunk by a man, whose warmth and coolness he alone knows.
Question: How does one apply effort while in motion?

Answer: Just as when still. While contemplation of the mind is not yet mature, there is a distinction between motion and stillness. Once it is mature, motion and stillness are no different. The Chan school says:
"Amid ten thousand people, as though there were not a single person; amid the turmoil of ten thousand affairs, as though there were not a single affair."

From this one may know that motion and stillness are one. Beginners have not yet attained concentration, and so the patriarchs teach people to tend and carry, meaning that in dealing with affairs and meeting people one should always tend and carry along this method of contemplating the mind. You need not be concerned; with long practice it becomes clear of itself. I quote a passage from the Lankavatara Sutra, to have it ready for your use. The sutra says:
"Contemplate all dharmas as without self-nature: like clouds in the sky, like a whirling wheel of fire, like a city of gandharvas, like an illusion, like a mirage
(like a dream, like a heat-haze)

, like the moon in water, like what is seen in a dream, never apart from one's own mind. Because of beginningless false views, one takes them to be external. Having contemplated thus, cut off the conditions of discrimination, and be free as well of the names and meanings that the deluded mind grasps. Know that the body, and things, and the place where one dwells, are all the realm of the store consciousness. There is no one who takes, and nothing taken, no arising, abiding, or ceasing. Reflecting thus, abide in it forever without letting go."

Savor this passage of scripture in the heart, and deep faith will arise. That you have not been able to do so has two causes: first, you are not yet familiar with the doctrine; second, the power of concentration is not yet accomplished. In short, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, you must never be apart from contemplation of the mind.
[Contemplating all dharmas as without self-nature]
Contemplate all dharmas: they are all phantasms.
The word self-nature has two meanings in Buddhist learning: first, the numinous power of wondrous illumination and myriad virtues
, and this is the self-nature of every living being and of every Buddha. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
"When self-nature is deluded, this is the living being; when self-nature is awakened, this is the Buddha."
(See
Mind, Self-Nature, and the Tathagatagarbha
; the second meaning is that of a real substance. The saying '
all

dharmas are without self-nature' means that all dharmas have no real substance and are all phantasms, like things in a dream. Being without self-nature is also called being without nature. The Treatise on Consciousness-Only says:
"All dharmas are without self-nature."
The Lotus Sutra says:
"Know that all dharmas are ever without nature."
The Surangama Sutra says:
"All phantasms become without nature."

[The whirling wheel of fire] In the darkness a man whirls a burning brand, and it is mistaken for a wheel of fire; this is used to illustrate a false appearance. [The city of gandharvas] The musicians are called gandharvas, and they can conjure towers and pavilions for people to behold; therefore these conjured towers are called a city of gandharvas. Phantasmal scenes such as a mirage over the sea are also called a city of gandharvas. [The heat-haze] The vapor produced beneath a blazing sun looks from afar like water; a thirsty deer longs to drink and runs after it, yet in the end can never reach it; this is used to illustrate an illusion. (See
Selected Notes on the Lankavatara Sutra

Question: I have already attained single-minded, undisturbed concentration in reciting the Buddha-name, and I now study the White Cloud Essentials of Mind in order to realize the mind and see the nature. But contemplation of the mind cannot be sustained, and it is harder still to contemplate the mind whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down. What shall I do?

Answer: You may proceed in two steps. First accomplish this: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, recite the Buddha-name without interruption and without distraction. Then raise a phrase of the Buddha-name and contemplate the mind for a while, raise the Buddha-name and contemplate for a while, and so on; in this way gradually pass over to complete contemplation of the mind, so that whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down you are never apart from contemplation of the mind.
